messages:
Anya Patel: Quick follow-up from the post-RFC sync on service auth surface. RFC asked for a migration path off monolithic project API keys — want to capture tradeoffs and a concrete path here.
Samir Rao: TL;DR: I still worry about blast radius if we keep reusing project keys for everything. Background jobs + user-facing requests on same token = bad.
Maya Chen: Agreed. The RFC leans toward brokered short-lived tokens for services. We need: claim layout, ACLs, audit trail, and a rollout plan that doesn't break existing clients.
Kevin Liu: Middle ground proposal: continue to allow existing project API keys, but provide a broker that mints short-lived service tokens. Runtime accepts both; service token preferred for attribution.
Anya Patel: How would RBAC checks map? Today checks use token.project and token.scopes. Service tokens need actor info and a binding to a project (if they act on behalf of a project).
Samir Rao: Keep token schema minimal: actor_type, actor_id, bound_project (optional), scopes, exp. Avoid embedding full role lists in token. Resolve roles at authz time.
Maya Chen: Important: tokens must be traceable. If svc A acts for project P, logs should show both actor_id and bound_project. That lets security audits attribute actions.
Kevin Liu: Broker API sketch (proto/CURL):
```
POST /v1/broker/mint
{
  "requester": "svc:billing-worker",
  "target_project": "proj-123",
  "ttl": 300
}
```
Response contains token with claims: {actor_type: "service", actor_id: "svc:billing-worker", bound_project: "proj-123", exp: <ts>}
Samir Rao: ACLs: broker should consult service-to-project allowlist (managed by infra teams). No implicit cross-project minting. Also rate-limit mint calls per service to avoid accidental token floods.
Anya Patel: Migration considerations:
- Phase 1: Broker exists, but runtimes accept both token types and continue to attribute to project when present.
- Phase 2: Encourage libraries (internal SDKs) to use broker for new services. Docs + quickstart.
- Phase 3: Deprecate use of project keys for service-to-service auth (long window).
Kevin Liu: Operational notes: broker must be highly available and low-latency. Consider an ephemeral token caching layer to avoid broker hot paths for each request. Also measure CPU/RPS for 1k services.
Maya Chen: Threat model quick notes:
- If a service token is leaked, TTL limits exposure.
- If broker is compromised, attacker can mint tokens — require mTLS + mfa for admin endpoints, rotate broker credentials via KMS/HSM.
Samir Rao: RBAC mapping during rollout: create a service role namespace (role:billing-worker) and map service identity -> roles via existing role-store. That avoids stuffing RBAC into tokens.
Anya Patel: Edge-case: third-party integrations where we can't run broker flow. For those, keep scoped long-lived tokens but restrict allowed actions and add more telemetry.
auth-bot: Note added to RFC-182 followups: action_items assigned (see thread).
Anya Patel: Action items: 1) Samir to draft token claim schema and sample JWT claims. 2) Kevin to prototype broker API and simple runtime acceptance logic. 3) Maya to produce a short threat model + ACL requirements doc.
Samir Rao: I'll take #1, aim to post a PR by EOD Fri.
Kevin Liu: I'll spin up a tiny PoC next week to show mint + validate flow.
Maya Chen: I'll draft the threat model + run it by infra sec.
Anya Patel: Cool. Let's reconvene next Tue 10am. Please drop any blockers here. :thumbsup:
